name: ground-control
description: One board for the GitHub issues you own and the Claude Code sessions running on your machine.

groundControl.github.logins.markdownDescription: Your GitHub username. Comma-separate several if you work under more than one account, such as a personal and a bot account. Left empty, the board offers to detect them from `gh auth status`.

groundControl.github.repo.markdownDescription: The repository work is tracked in, as `owner/name`. The board reads no work until this is set, and says so.

groundControl.github.projectNumber.description: The GitHub project board work is tracked on. Used when Card Source is 'project'.

enumDescriptions: Only issues on the configured project board. The board reports how many assigned issues this excludes.
Every open issue assigned to you, whether or not it is on the board.

groundControl.github.ghPath.description: Path to the GitHub CLI, if it is not on PATH.

groundControl.boardStatuses.markdownDescription: Which project-board statuses keep an issue on the board; anything not listed is archived behind the Show-archived toggle. Editing this list clears the Returned marks, and removing a status archives its cards, which then forget which lane you had put them in. Where a card lands is `#groundControl.statusLanes#`, your own open pull requests, and your own placement.

groundControl.statusLanes.markdownDescription: Which lane a card arrives in — and stays in until you move it — for the statuses that carry one. A status that says nothing about stage is left out. A status mapped to `build` outranks your pull request, because work comes back to you as a reassignment rather than as a review asking for changes; for every other lane your own **open** pull request outranks this, and a merged or closed one is read as nothing. A card you have moved yourself is never moved again, until it goes past your hands and comes back. Card triage reads the same map for what a status *means*: `review` is a card to review, `unstarted` one to begin, and `build` or a status left out leaves the label to the pull request and the conversation.

groundControl.sessionRefreshSeconds.description: How often the board re-reads the agent sessions on this machine, while it is the visible tab. Each read spawns the agent CLI, so a short interval costs a process every few seconds.

groundControl.agents.markdownDescription: The agent CLIs to read sessions from, as id to command or full path — `claude` and `codex`. Leave this empty unless a CLI is somewhere the board would not find it: the board detects what is installed, so Claude is always read and Codex is read whenever it has a home of its own. Naming any agent replaces what was detected, so name every one you want: an agent left out is not read, and its session hooks are not installed.

groundControl.branchIssuePattern.markdownDescription: Matches the issue number in a branch or directory name, as a regular expression whose first capture group is the number. The team convention ships as the default.

groundControl.refreshIntervalSeconds.description: How often the board refreshes while it is open.

groundControl.hosts.markdownDescription: Which editor applications the board may reach into. An id the board does not know is named above the lanes rather than silently reaching nothing.

groundControl.sources.markdownDescription: Where the board reads work from. An id the board does not know is named above the lanes rather than silently reading nothing.

groundControl.triage.enabled.markdownDescription: Work out what each card is waiting on when it arrives, and label it with that plus one sentence saying where the card stands. It reads the recent comments on the issue and its pull request; it never moves a card and never writes anything anywhere. **This sends that text — including other people's comments and logins — to the model's API**, which is the one thing the board does that leaves your machine, and **it spends your own Claude usage**: the first board you open reads every card on it. It runs only while a board is open, a couple at a time. Turning it off stops new readings; the labels already on your cards stay, and stop being refreshed.

groundControl.triage.model.markdownDescription: The model that classifies a card. Give a full model name rather than an alias — an alias that quietly resolves elsewhere changes both what it costs and how well it reads. A name Claude Code does not know fails every card, which the board says above the lanes.

groundControl.triage.names.markdownDescription: Who a GitHub login really is, where GitHub's own answer is not the person — an agent account whose profile names the agent rather than whoever drives it, or somebody whose profile carries no name. Key is the login, value is the name to use: `{ "buildfriday": "Chris" }`. Everyone else is named from their GitHub profile, and a login with neither is shown as the login. Cards name people by their first name.

groundControl.triage.concurrency.markdownDescription: How many cards are read at once. The first time you open a board every card is read, so this is what decides whether that arrives as a trickle or all at once.

groundControl.triage.timeoutSeconds.markdownDescription: How long one card gets, covering both reading it from GitHub and classifying it. Real cards measured 27 to 102 seconds — how long a card takes tracks how much has been written on it — so the default leaves room for the slow end. A card that runs over is left unread, and its chip tries again.

groundControl.actions.merge-upstream.ena.markdownDescription: Whether the board runs `#groundControl.actions.merge-upstream.prompt#` on a card asking for the **base branch merged into yours**, without waiting to be pressed. It does nothing until that prompt is set — there is no shipped default, because what merges a branch is your own repository's skill. Off, the card carries a control that runs the same prompt when you press it. The board never merges on its own reading of a stale branch: the card has to be asking for a merge.

groundControl.actions.merge-upstream.pro.markdownDescription: What a merge-upstream session is told to do. **Setting this puts a control on the card that starts an agent in your checkout and may push**, whether or not `#groundControl.actions.merge-upstream.enabled#` is on. A prompt beginning with `/` is a slash command, e.g. `/or-merge {base} {branch} {issue} --single`. The board fills `{issue}`, `{repo}`, `{pr}`, `{branch}`, `{base}`, `{checkout}` and `{resultPath}` — write a small JSON `{ "outcome": "pushed"|"halted", "detail": "…", "auditPath": "…" }` to `{resultPath}`. **That file is the verdict**: `pushed` is what the card reports as **Merged**, and a run that writes nothing reads as stopped short. The board does not re-read GitHub to check — the base branch moves under a card within minutes, so a conflict somebody else landed afterwards would read as your run having failed. It refuses a pull request based on anything but the repository's default branch, because keeping a stacked branch current is a chain of merges it cannot order — and a card with no checkout it has seen a session run in, because it will not guess a directory from a branch name.

groundControl.actions.permissionMode.markdownDescription: What a session the board starts may do without asking. `auto` is the default because it is the narrowest mode a background run actually finishes under: `manual` and `acceptEdits` park on the first `git` command with a permission prompt nobody is there to answer, `dontAsk` denies it outright, and `plan` cannot write at all — a card under any of those reads as **Working** until the run is stopped. `bypassPermissions` turns the permission system off entirely, and means the session runs whatever it likes in that checkout.

groundControl.actions.concurrency.markdownDescription: How many card actions run at once. These are real builds in real checkouts, so the default is one.

groundControl.actions.dailyLimit.markdownDescription: How many actions the board may start in a rolling 24 hours, however many cards ask for one. This is the ceiling on a mistake: a rule that fires more often than you expected costs this many sessions and then stops. Zero stops the board acting on its own entirely, and leaves each card's control working.

groundControl.actions.resultMinutes.markdownDescription: How long a dispatch whose session never appeared on the machine is left open before the board calls it lost. Not a limit on the work — a run is followed until its session ends, however long that takes.

groundControl.newSession.prompt.markdownDescription: What a session started from a card is prefilled with. It lands in the composer unsent — you send it, or clear it. `{issue}`, `{repo}`, `{title}`, `{url}` and `{checkout}` are replaced with the card's own; anything else in braces is left as typed. Empty starts a bare session. Codex offers no way in that takes a prompt, so a Codex session starts bare whatever this says.

groundControl.logLevel.markdownDescription: How much the background process writes about what it is doing. `info` is one line per source read, per board that connects, per card moved and per run started. `debug` adds one line per `gh` call with its duration, per session read, and per activity marker batch — useful when the board is slow or empty and you want to see where the time goes. Neither setting can silence the process starting, stopping, or refusing a request: those are always written. The log is at `~/.claude/ground-control/hub.log`, and **Ground Control: Show Logs** opens it live.

groundControl.installSessionHooks.markdownDescription: Let the board tell when a session is running. Neither CLI reports what an interactive session is doing, so the board writes a small activity hook per agent — `~/.claude/ground-control/hook.mjs` with entries in `~/.claude/settings.json`, and `~/.claude/ground-control/codex-hook.mjs` with entries in `~/.codex/hooks.json` — for the agents on this machine, the first time you open the board. It backs each file up first, adds only its own entries, and refuses to write at all if it cannot read one. Codex runs a hook only once it has been told to trust it, so the board asks Codex to trust its own entries and nothing else — through Codex, which writes its own `config.toml`. Turn this off to remove every entry — sessions still appear, they just cannot report what they are doing.

groundControl.openWindowsForSessions.markdownDescription: Whether opening a session may bring another VS Code window forward or open a new one to resume a historical session. A session is only reachable from the window showing it, so this is what lets the board cross windows — at the cost of moving your focus. An active session requires its existing window. A historical session may open a new window on its saved directory. Off, a session held elsewhere is named and refused instead.
